message: Hi pcmattman ;-)
Hello kwolf

Or do you filter all of our mails directly into the spam folder? ;-)
Ah, I have them
Nah, they got lost in the flood of QEMU emails :)
Ah, you don't filter at all, it seems?
I don't
I have decent full-text search on my email though, so it's ok
So the CDI sound layer is an interface between the OS and the sound hardware?
Right
If I understand right from looking at this, there's no mixer or anything like that?
I think it would live outside the driver
It's the same for all devices anyway, right?
I agree with that, I just wanted to be sure
I mean if you want to have some shared mixer code I'm all for it, but it doesn't belong into the driver interface
Yup, that's why I was checking. I'd think the mixer et al would be quite host-specific, so they shouldn't be done via CDI
Unless there is a hardware mixer. But I think we can keep it simple for now.
kwolf: One thing I did want to mention, related to the CDI network code
As far as I can tell there's no way to tell if the NIC is actually connected to a network in the current interface
I think you're right
Would you like to propose an interface?
It's a little tricky, but I'm going to be implementing it for our native driver interface in the next couple of days
Once I've got that sorted I'll get a patch together for CDI, to see what I can put together
You probably need to poll the state?
Probably end up being something like "link_state_t cdi_net_link_state(device)" where link_state_t is an enum of different link states
Some NICs will be able to store it as a variable, others will just return a "connected" value (no method to find out link state), and others will have to read registers
I know some can fire an IRQ when the link state changes, which backs up storing as a variable
I guess it's driver-dependent, as long as the cdi_net_link_state function is implemented and returns valid data :)
It would be more convenient for the OS to have a callback interface then
Possibly, but that only works if the device can fire an IRQ to tell the driver that the link state has changed
Right. But if it can, polling would be wasted work.
I was thinking that the host would initiate the communication, requesting the link state from the driver
We can start with the polling interface, adding a callback later is still possible
You would mainly be doing something like "if(cdi_new_link_state(device) != connected) { some_sort_of_error; }"
NICs which can use an IRQ will store link state in a variable and simply return that variable, others will have to talk to the NIC
Hm, there could be more information that just connected or not, like link speed etc. Maybe make cdi_link_state_t a struct?
pcmattman: Right, that makes sense
Hm, good point
So the link state is more or less a structure, containing information about whether there's a connection or not and link speed
And anything else we still forgot ;-)
I'll be back in a couple of hours
Ok, maybe Max will be here then, too
re and hello @ all

Hi XanClic
Good afternoon
Should I translate all the comments to English?
I think a while ago we decided to have them bilingual
With some doxygen config option to switch the language
Oh, so how do you do it with doxygen comments?
Something like bluecode did for the liblightc++ beginnings
Basically it was the doxygen version of #ifdef GERMAN
Anyway, let's get the audio interface right first. I think the most important point is if cdi_audio_driver.act is what we want.
I thought, the operating system has one buffer which is refreshed all the time.
If calls one time act() with this buffer as a parameter and CDI_AUDIO_LOOP
-If +It
Hm, ok... I didn't even understand that changing the buffer was allowed while it's being played ;-)
No, it would not be
But I still need to keep in sync what the card is playing right now and where I'm inserting new data
Yeah, that's a problem
XanClic: It wouldn't be allowed? Then how is looping going to help?
If you call act() when there's stuff being played, then this old operation would be canceled
-1 is returned, if you gave act() bad parameters or something like this
Or just if the hardware fails
Right, but obviously I don't want to skip the old buffer. I usually just want to add some more data at the end
Then you have to loop ;-)
And insert it at the beginning
But that's right, there must be a function that returns the position in the current buffer or something like this
Would definitely be helpful

And act and that looping thing is underdocumented. I still don't understand what really happens. It copies the data into some hardware buffers and only when everything played and we're looping it'll re-read the user buffer?
That's right.
pcmattman: How do you feel about this?
I didn't write how I thought this should be used, because that's not the problem of the interface CDI - OS, but of the interface OS - User
*CDI driver
Well, which data is copied when is a basic part of the driver interface
kwolf: " If you call act() when there's stuff being played, then this old operation would be canceled" <-- That's logical, the OS itself would control the operations and when to send
I'm not arguing that it's insane, but I wasn't clear to me that it works this way
Ah, I understand
However, I'm not sure if it's really easy to use this way
Because you would need to provide a new buffer that starts exactly at the point where the sound card is when you call act()
Perhaps act() should push onto a queue then?
Don't think that helps. We need some way to replace data that is already sent
Say I send 5 seconds to the card and after one second another sound needs to be played
Hmm, true
Not sure how the best interface for such a replacement would look like
I unfortunately don't know enough about sound devices to be able to talk intelligently about how to do that specific example
Neither do I ;-)
I just know that I want the first sound to be played without a short pause or skipping a small part
XanClic: Did you have plans how to implement this?
It all depends on whether sound data is sent to the card in full or if it's sent in blocks every <n> ticks
How do you send an internet radio stream to the card in full?
The question is how large the blocks are, but chances are that you still need to replace them when they are already sent to the card
Unless you want to wait for sounds for a second (or how long one block will be)
What I meant is a block being a tiny frame of a sound
In my naive understanding of how this works, it'd be something like sending data to the card many times each second
No, that can't be right, it'd be horribly slow in practice
Won't making the sound blocks tiny increase the CPU usage?
I think XanClic mentioned something like with ac97 he could submit like 30 seconds at once
So if that buffer is DMA'd, you're saying make it possible to modify that buffer live?
Not sure if you would just modify the buffer or stop the soundcard, point to the new buffer and start again
Shouldn't make a big difference for the interface, though
It should be no problem to modify the buffer given to the card via act() after calling this function
So you could give the buffer to the card driver and if you want to play other stuff after a second, you could replace the content of the buffer at this point
Sounds good to me
That was my idea when I wrote "#define CDI_AUDIO_LOOP 1" ;-)
Ok
The blocks really sent to an AC97 card have a duration of... 0,37 seconds.
I guess we need to implement it to see if it works out, but it sounds reasonable at least
XanClic: I'm afraid this means implementing a mixer ;-)
Of course it does ;-)
Well then, have fun ;-)
You also could enqueue all request, so you don't actually need to "mix" something, but the sound driver card won't do that
xD
*sound card driver
"sound driver card", also interesting. A card designed for a sound driver *g*
No, a card producing sound drivers. We definitely need to buy one.
Night
